previous_disclosures.section: OTHER RISKS > FFIEC-Cross-Border Claims on Third Parties and Local Country Assets
previous_disclosures.summary: Citigroup's cross-border disclosures follow Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council (FFIEC) guidelines, where exposure amounts are based on the domicile of the ultimate obligor and exclude the benefit of collateral received for secured transactions. Netting of derivatives is permitted only under legally binding agreements with the same counterparty, and credit default swaps are included based on gross notional amounts.

comparisons.peer_summary: Non-U.S. exposure includes sovereign and non-sovereign credit, securities, and investments on an internal risk management basis, comprising funded loans, unfunded commitments, net counterparty exposure from derivatives and financing transactions, and securities netted to zero, with net country exposure adjusted for hedges and credit protection.
comparisons.comparison: Both Citi and Bank of America disclose methodologies for measuring country or cross-border exposure, but they diverge significantly on the treatment of collateral and hedges. Citi explicitly states under FFIEC guidelines that amounts do not consider the benefit of collateral for secured financing transactions and do not include the benefit of margin or hedges (Sentence S004, S005). In contrast, Bank of America's internal risk management basis for non-U.S. exposure explicitly includes net country exposure adjusted for 'hedges and credit default protection purchased, net of credit default protection sold' (Sentence S005), indicating a substantive difference in risk mitigation recognition where BAC nets protections while Citi reports gross of hedges for regulatory reporting.

sentences.text: • Amounts do not consider the benefit of collateral received for secured financing transactions (i.e., repurchase agreements, reverse repurchase agreements and securities loaned and borrowed) and are reported based on notional amounts.

• Netting of derivative receivables and payables, reported at fair value, is permitted, but only under a legally binding netting agreement with the same specific counterparty, and does not include the benefit of margin received or hedges.
Net country exposure represents country exposure less hedges and credit default protection purchased, net of credit default protection sold.

comparisons.peer_summary: The firm bears credit risk in securities financing transactions to the extent that cash or collateral provided exceeds what is received, with collateral primarily consisting of government obligations, as detailed in a table showing concentrations by industry, region, and rating.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures address credit risk in securities financing transactions (such as repos and securities lending) and the role of collateral. Citi specifies that under FFIEC guidelines, amounts for these transactions do not consider the benefit of collateral and are reported based on notional amounts (Sentence S004). Goldman Sachs similarly describes bearing credit risk only to the extent that cash advanced or securities pledged exceeds the value of collateral received (Sentence S003, S004), but notes that the table reflects netting agreements and collateral considered when determining credit risk, implying a management view that differs from Citi's strict regulatory gross reporting.

sentences.text: • Amounts do not consider the benefit of collateral received for secured financing transactions (i.e., repurchase agreements, reverse repurchase agreements and securities loaned and borrowed) and are reported based on notional amounts.

We bear credit risk related to resale agreements and securities borrowed only to the extent that cash advanced or the value of securities pledged or delivered to the counterparty exceeds the value of the collateral received.

We also have credit exposure on repurchase agreements and securities loaned to the extent that the value of securities pledged or delivered to the counterparty for these transactions exceeds the amount of cash or collateral received.

comparisons.peer_topic: Netting and Collateral Definitions for OTC Derivatives
comparisons.peer_summary: OTC derivative assets are reported on a net-by-counterparty basis when legal rights of setoff exist and fair value is net of cash collateral received. Collateral includes cash and securities (primarily government obligations) received under credit support agreements, which are considered in credit risk determination but are not eligible for netting under U.S. GAAP.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures discuss netting of derivatives and the treatment of collateral. Citi allows netting of derivative receivables and payables only under a legally binding netting agreement with the same specific counterparty, explicitly excluding the benefit of margin received or hedges (Sentence S005). Goldman Sachs reports OTC derivative assets on a net-by-counterparty basis when legal rights of setoff exist and accounts for fair value net of cash collateral received (Sentence S002). While both utilize legal netting agreements, Citi's regulatory exclusion of margin benefits contrasts with GS's accounting practice of netting cash collateral received.

sentences.text: • Netting of derivative receivables and payables, reported at fair value, is permitted, but only under a legally binding netting agreement with the same specific counterparty, and does not include the benefit of margin received or hedges.

• OTC derivative assets, included in the consolidated balance sheets, are reported on a net-by-counterparty basis (i.e., the net receivable for a given counterparty) when a legal right of setoff exists under an enforceable netting agreement (counterparty netting) and are accounted for at fair value, net of cash collateral received under enforceable credit support agreements (cash collateral netting).

comparisons.peer_topic: Specific measurement methods for country risk components
comparisons.peer_summary: The Firm measures specific exposures such as bank deposits at cash balances, lending at committed amounts net of collateral, securities at fair value, and derivatives at fair value net of collateral, with credit derivatives at net notional amount.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures detail the measurement of specific exposure components like lending and derivatives, but apply different adjustments for collateral. Citi reports amounts based on FFIEC guidelines which do not consider the benefit of collateral for secured transactions and exclude margin/hedges (Sentence S004, S005). JPMorgan's internal framework measures lending exposures at the committed amount net of eligible cash and marketable securities collateral (Sentence S003) and counterparty exposure on derivatives at fair value net of eligible collateral (Sentence S006). This represents a key difference where JPM's internal risk management nets collateral for measurement, whereas Citi's cited regulatory reporting does not.

sentences.text: • Amounts do not consider the benefit of collateral received for secured financing transactions (i.e., repurchase agreements, reverse repurchase agreements and securities loaned and borrowed) and are reported based on notional amounts.

• Netting of derivative receivables and payables, reported at fair value, is permitted, but only under a legally binding netting agreement with the same specific counterparty, and does not include the benefit of margin received or hedges.
• Lending exposures are measured at the total committed amount (funded and unfunded), net of the allowance for credit losses and eligible cash and marketable securities collateral received
• Counterparty exposure on derivative receivables is measured at the derivative's fair value, net of the fair value of the eligible collateral received

comparisons.peer_summary: Net counterparty exposure from transactions like repurchase agreements and OTC derivatives is calculated net of collateral received and net by counterparty where master netting agreements apply.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures define net counterparty exposure in the context of securities financing and derivatives, highlighting differences in collateral treatment. Citi's FFIEC-based reporting does not consider the benefit of collateral for secured financing transactions (Sentence S004). Morgan Stanley explicitly states that net counterparty exposure is calculated 'net of the benefit of collateral received' (Sentence S001). This indicates that while both peers manage counterparty risk, MS's defined metric for net exposure includes collateral benefits, whereas Citi's cited regulatory disclosure excludes them.
